sections.overview: A small toothed whale of northern temperate and subarctic seas, the harbour porpoise ranges across coastal and shelf waters of the North Atlantic and North Pacific, with separate regional forms in the Black Sea. Populations differ in distribution and prey, so local evidence matters when describing this widespread species.
sections.identification: The compact adult has a rounded head without a long beak, dark grey back, paler flanks and light underside. Its low triangular dorsal fin sits near mid-back; small pointed pectoral flippers and flattened, spade-shaped teeth distinguish its form. Females are generally larger; throat markings vary. British adults are typically 145–160 cm and 50–55 kg; females grow larger, reaching about 189 cm and 81 kg, versus 163 cm and 54 kg for males.
sections.habitat: It mainly inhabits cold-temperate and subarctic coastal and shelf waters, including bays, estuaries and fjords. The University of British Columbia reports typical depths to about 150 m, though deeper sightings occur. In Europe it is widespread around the North Sea and British Isles, but patchier in the Baltic and Iberian Atlantic.
sections.diet: Its diet varies by place, season and year. It takes small fish from both the water column and seabed; herring, capelin, sandeels, whiting or cod dominate in different regions. Squid and other invertebrates supplement the diet. Porpoises in one locality often rely chiefly on a few fish species and swallow prey whole.
sections.behavior: Usually alone or in small groups, harbour porpoises surface in a low rolling motion and rarely approach moving boats. Echolocation clicks guide navigation and prey detection; rapid click bursts help focus on targets. Seasonal shifts occur in some areas, but coordinated long-distance migration is not generally evident.
sections.reproduction: Maturity is usually reached at three to four years. Following summer mating, gestation lasts about 10–11 months and usually yields one calf. Birth season varies: May–July in the Bay of Fundy and Scottish waters, June–August in the German North Sea and Baltic. Calves begin solid food around five months and nurse about eight or nine months.
sections.ecology: Feeding on small pelagic and bottom-associated fish connects prey communities to this coastal marine predator. Killer whales and large sharks prey on porpoises; fatal attacks by bottlenose dolphins are also documented. Its use of productive coastal grounds overlaps with fisheries and vessel traffic, exposing it to bycatch and underwater noise.
sections.conservation: The 2020 IUCN global assessment classified the species as Least Concern, while identifying the Baltic subpopulation as Critically Endangered. Black Sea populations are assessed separately. A UK assessment published in 2026 rated status Unfavourable-inadequate nationally and Unfavourable-bad in the Celtic and Irish Seas unit for 2019–24. Gillnet bycatch, noise, pollution and prey depletion are pressures.
